claims.claim: Nearly all quartz watches use a crystal oscillating at 32,768 Hz - a power of two (2^15) chosen so simple binary counters can derive a one-second pulse.
claims.episode_span: A quartz crystal cut to precise dimensions and excited by a small voltage vibrates at 32,768 cycles per second, a frequency high enough for one-second resolution yet low enough to be divided by a simple chain of binary counters.
claims.supporting_quote: This frequency is a power of two ( 32 768 = 2 15 ), just high enough to exceed the human hearing range , yet low enough to keep electric energy consumption , cost and size at a modest level and to permit inexpensive counters to derive a 1-second pulse.

claims.claim: A chain of 15 divide-by-two flip-flop stages reduces the 32,768 Hz signal to a once-per-second pulse.
claims.episode_span: the quartz divider chain performs its fifteen successive halvings of 32,768 Hz in a single etched silicon die
claims.supporting_quote: The output from that is fed into a second flip-flop, and so on through a chain of 15 flip-flops, each of which acts as an effective power of 2 frequency divider by dividing the frequency of the input signal by 2.

claims.claim: In analog quartz watches a stepping motor converts the one-pulse-per-second electronic output into mechanical motion of the hands.
claims.episode_span: the only remaining mechanical task was advancing the hands once per second, which a tiny stepper motor could accomplish with a single part instead of dozens
claims.supporting_quote: In analog quartz clocks and wristwatches, the electric pulse-per-second output is nearly always transferred to a Lavet-type stepping motor that converts the electronic input pulses from the flip-flops counting unit into mechanical output that can be used to move hands.

claims.claim: Standard quartz watch accuracy is on the order of seconds per month: a typical quartz wristwatch gains or loses about 15 seconds per 30 days.
claims.episode_span: its accuracy surpassed anything the old mechanical craft could sustain at comparable price
claims.supporting_quote: a typical quartz clock or wristwatch will gain or lose 15 seconds per 30 days (within a normal temperature range of 5 to 35 °C or 41 to 95 °F ) or less than a half second clock drift per day when worn near the body

claims.claim: Quartz watches, introduced in 1969 (Seiko Astron), largely replaced mechanical watches worldwide during the 1970s and 1980s.
claims.episode_span: That single substitution collapsed the cost curve of reliable timekeeping and left an entire national industry without a product that anyone needed to buy for the sake of knowing the hour.
claims.supporting_quote: The quartz crisis (Switzerland) or quartz revolution (United States, Japan, and other countries) was the upheaval in the watchmaking industry caused by the advent of quartz watches in the 1970s and 1980s, that largely replaced mechanical watches around the world.

claims.claim: The quartz crisis devastated the Swiss watch industry: Swiss watch employment fell from 90,000 to 28,000 between 1970 and 1988.
claims.episode_span: left an entire national industry without a product that anyone needed to buy for the sake of knowing the hour
claims.supporting_quote: Between 1970 and 1988, Swiss watch employment fell from 90,000 to 28,000.

claims.claim: Swiss producers survived by repositioning mechanical watches as luxury goods valued for craftsmanship and heritage rather than timekeeping utility.
claims.episode_span: Swiss producers survived by repositioning their remaining mechanical output as objects whose value lay in finishing, rarity, and heritage rather than in daily timekeeping utility.
claims.supporting_quote: Mechanical watches have gradually become luxury goods appreciated for their elaborate craftsmanship, aesthetic appeal, and glamorous design, sometimes associated with the social status of their owners, rather than simple timekeeping devices.
